title: On Holding $ONON: I Bought the Shoes First, Then the Stock
snippet: There is an old Peter Lynch line that I keep coming back to: some of the best ideas are sitting in your own house.
content_html:
There is an old Peter Lynch line that I keep coming back to: some of the best ideas are sitting in your own house. Not because “buy what you know” is a substitute for analysis — it never is — but because personal use gives you a data point that no spreadsheet does. You know whether the thing is actually good.

I own two pairs of On. One is my running shoe. The other has quietly become my everyday shoe — the one I put on to walk into town, to travel, to do nothing in particular. Both are Swiss, both are expensive, and both are more comfortable than anything else in my hallway. And here is the part that matters as an investor: my running pair is on its way out. It always is. Somewhere between six and twelve months, depending on the winter, the foam gives up and I go buy another one.

That sentence is the whole investment case in miniature, and it is the reason I prefer On to a company like Lululemon. Leggings and technical tops last years. Foam does not. A running shoe is a consumable dressed up as a durable good — the customer comes back on a schedule set by physics, not by fashion. When a brand with that replacement cycle also owns the customer relationship directly, you get something rare in consumer: recurring revenue without a subscription.

So when the stock fell out of bed after the second quarter, I bought a first small position for the Haas Invest4 Innovation Fund.

The short version. On Holding AG (NYSE: ONON) trades at $27.99, a market capitalisation of roughly $9.4 billion, within a whisker of its 52-week low of $27.56 and about 56% below the all-time high of $64.05 set in January 2025. The business behind that price grew constant-currency net sales 21.6% in Q2 2026, expanded gross margin to 65.4% — the best in the industry — carries CHF 1.2 billion in cash and not one franc of financial debt, and is run again, since May, by its own founders. On my numbers the stock changes hands at roughly 17x this year’s adjusted earnings and 19xowner earnings after deducting share-based compensation. Against a fair P/E of 23 and 18% organic growth, that is an expected return of about 19% per year.

The market is pricing a brand that is running out of road. The quarter showed a company deliberately taking its foot off one pedal to protect the other. Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them is the opportunity.

1. Product, business model, brand and moat

What it actually is

On began in 2010 in Zurich, when Olivier Bernhard — a former professional triathlete — was told it was physically impossible to cut holes into the rubber sole of a running shoe, and did it anyway. That became CloudTec, the hollow-chamber sole that still defines the silhouette. Bernhard brought in David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti, two marketing men, and the three of them built a brand that sixteen years later sells in more than 90 countries.

Shoes are still roughly 92% of the business. Apparel is about 6% and accessories are the rest. On is not a shoe company that also does fashion; it is a shoe company with a young and very fast-growing apparel line attached. I want to correct my own first instinct here, because it matters for how you underwrite the thing: apparel grew 56% at constant currency last quarter, which is spectacular, but from CHF 54 million on a CHF 850 million quarter. It is a category option, not yet a second leg.

The verticals are performance running, outdoor, training, tennis, all-day and a young-movers line. Training grew 40% last quarter behind the Cloudpulse and Cloud X franchises. Tennis apparel nearly tripled. Cloudtilt — the lifestyle sneaker — took three of the top five selling slots at Foot Locker Europe and rose 190% in the premium sneaker channel.

How the money is made

Two channels. Wholesale (54% of Q2 sales) sells through run-specialty stores, sporting goods chains and, increasingly, luxury and street-fashion retail. Direct-to-consumer (46%) is on.com, the On app, and a growing network of owned stores — the Champs-Élysées flagship was the best-performing location in the world last quarter, and On opened its first shops in São Paulo and Copenhagen in recent weeks.

The economics of the mix shift are the entire margin story. DTC captures the retailer’s margin, and On refuses to discount. Coppetti described the pricing architecture on the last call: entry at around $160, the mid-range at $200 to $210, and the top of the range pushing toward $300 — with LightSpray products selling at $290 and selling out. Gross margin has moved from the low 60s to 65.4%, and management raised full-year guidance to at least 65% while absorbing US import tariffs and excluding any refunds. Very few consumer companies on earth run at that level.

The brand

Global aided awareness is now 30%. That number is the single most important figure in this analysis, and it cuts both ways. It means On has become genuinely famous. It also means seven out of ten people worldwide still have never heard of it. Nike’s awareness is effectively saturated. On has sold roughly 50 million pairs of shoes in its entire history — Nike ships more than that in a good quarter.

The demographic direction is right, too: consumers under 34 are now more than a third of the customer base, up sharply, helped by the Zendaya co-created collection (every US style beat internal forecasts by triple digits) and a Loewe collaboration that put On on a different kind of shelf entirely. Roger Federer has been an investor and product partner since 2019, and the Roland-Garros visibility feeds directly into Paris retail. This is a brand being built on two axes at once — performance credibility with runners, cultural credibility with everyone else — and the second axis is what turns a running shoe company into a global sportswear brand.

The moat

Let me be honest about the weakest part of the case: there is no structural moat here in the way there is in software.Anyone can make a shoe. Nike, Adidas, Asics, Brooks, New Balance, Hoka and Salomon all make good ones. The barriers are brand, distribution and manufacturing know-how, and every one of them is scalable by a competitor with enough money.

What On has instead is a set of advantages that are hard rather than impossible to copy:

  • Design signature. A CloudTec sole is identifiable across a street. That is worth more than a patent.

  • Manufacturing IP. LightSpray sprays a one-piece upper in minutes using a robotic arm. It is scaling out of Busan and Zurich, it collapses the supply chain and the labour content, and it is now selling commercially rather than sitting in a lab. Nobody else has it.

  • Price discipline as a strategy. Refusing to discount is not a policy, it is a moat you build every quarter and lose in one. On is currently choosing lower reported growth to protect it. More on that below.

  • Channel control. Every point of DTC mix is a point of margin and a point of customer data that a wholesale partner would otherwise own.

Hoka is the cautionary comparison. Same origin story, one year earlier, founded in the French Alps. Hoka scaled through wholesale and run-specialty at speed and is now decelerating hard in the US. On took the slower road — own stores, own app, full price — and is the one still compounding above 20%.

2. The market

Global athletic footwear is somewhere in the region of $145–155 billion, growing mid-single digits. Estimates from the various research houses vary enormously depending on what they include, so I treat the absolute number as directional only. Running shoes are roughly a third of it, and North America is the largest region at about a third of global spend.

Three characteristics matter for the investment case:

It is huge relative to On. At CHF 3.5 billion of expected 2026 sales, On has somewhere around 2% of global athletic footwear. Nike does close to $46 billion. This is not a company that runs out of market — it runs out of execution or it does not.

The growth is not in the market, it is in the share shift. The category itself compounds at 5%. On compounds at 20%+ because it is taking share from incumbents who neglected premium running for a decade. On and Hoka together now hold roughly 19% of the US premium running market, from nothing. That share shift is the thesis, and it has a natural ceiling — which is why I do not underwrite 20% growth in perpetuity.

Political exposure is real but improving. This is a discretionary consumer product manufactured mostly in Asia and sold heavily into the United States, which is about 53% of sales. Tariffs hit it directly. The good news arrived in February, when the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs 6-3, ruling that the President lacked authority to impose them. On has filed for refunds, has said it will reinvest the proceeds rather than pass them through, and — critically — has excluded every franc of expected refunds from its guidance. The refund machinery at Customs is slow and messy, but this is a live, unpriced, positive optionality.

Cyclicality is the honest weakness. A CHF 250 shoe is a discretionary purchase, and in a real consumer recession people wear last year’s pair for another six months. On’s premium positioning and affluent customer base have shielded it so far, but they will not shield it forever. This is a beta-2.08 stock and it will behave like one.

3. Culture and management

In March, On announced that CEO Martin Hoffmann would step down after thirteen years — five of them as CEO, having joined as CFO to bring financial discipline to a chaotic startup. From 1 May, co-founders David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti took over as Co-CEOs, while remaining Executive Co-Chairmen of the Board. Olivier Bernhard stays on as an executive board member. Scott Maguire, previously chief innovation officer, was promoted to President and COO. Frank Sluis joined as CFO.

The market did not like it. The stock fell 10% on the day, and analysts complained about churn — Marc Maurer had left the year before, now Hoffmann. HSBC flagged the timing and the absence of an external hire.

I read it the other way, and this is where my framework and the market’s diverge most sharply. I want founder-led companies. The overwhelming majority of the businesses I own are run by the people who started them, because founders make decisions on a decade horizon and hired managers make them on a quarterly one. On explicitly framed the change as protecting “entrepreneurial speed” and putting the founders’ long-term stewardship into direct alignment with execution.

You could see the difference within twelve weeks. Allemann opened the Q2 call not with numbers but with the story of breaking the industry’s moulds to make CloudTec — and then, in the same breath, told investors that On was deliberately limiting wholesale shipments because it would not build in-channel inventory that compromises full-price integrity. That is a founder decision. A professional CEO twelve weeks into the job protects the guidance and ships the shoes. These men own the company, they have owned it for sixteen years, and they are optimising for what the brand is worth in 2036.

The evidence that the culture still produces is on the product side, not the slide deck. The CloudX 5 with its CleanCloud midsole has passed a million pairs produced — four years ahead of the internal target. Every everyday running franchise will be re-platformed onto new foams and fit engineering within fourteen months, which Sluis called the fastest product rollout in the company’s history. Spring/Summer 2027 orders for the Cloudsurfer 3 doubled from retail partners after the inaugural Running Summit in Paris.

4. Financials, margins, and where the trend is going

The revenue arc

Net sales went CHF 1.79 billion (2023) → CHF 2.32 billion (2024) → CHF 3.01 billion (2025, +30%). Guidance for 2026 is low-20s constant-currency growth, implying CHF 3.47–3.56 billion. Revenue has more than quadrupled since the 2021 IPO.

The first half of 2026 delivered CHF 1,682 million, +24.0% at constant currency but only +14.0% as reported — a ten-point gap created entirely by the Swiss franc. On earns in dollars, yen and euros, and reports in one of the strongest currencies on earth. At roughly 0.81 USD/CHF, that translation drag is a permanent tax on reported results, and it is a big part of why the headline numbers look weaker than the business is.

By region in Q2 (constant currency): Asia-Pacific +54.7%, EMEA +20.5%, Americas +13.0%. APAC is now over 20% of global sales, driven by Japan, South Korea and Greater China. The geographic mix is de-risking on its own.

The margin stack

For the half year, gross margin was 64.8% and adjusted EBITDA margin 20.3%, on CHF 342 million of adjusted EBITDA. Full-year guidance holds adjusted EBITDA margin at 19.5–20.0% while raising gross margin to at least 65%, which tells you the incremental gross profit is being reinvested into stores, marketing and product rather than dropped to the bottom line. At this stage of the brand’s life, that is the right call.

Reported net income is noisy and you should treat it carefully. The Q2 2025 loss of CHF 40.9 million was not an operating problem — it was an unrealised FX revaluation of CHF 139.9 million when the dollar hit multi-decade lows against the franc. Strip the currency noise and the underlying earnings power has been rising steadily throughout. H1 2026 net income was CHF 208.3 million against CHF 15.8 million a year earlier; adjusted net income was CHF 241.1 million against CHF 40.9 million.

Return on equity on trailing twelve-month earnings is roughly 22% on average equity — and that is understated, because CHF 1.2 billion of idle cash sits in the denominator earning very little.

The balance sheet and cash

This is the part that lets me sleep. Cash of CHF 1,205.6 million at 30 June, up 18% in six months, against zero financial debt (there are CHF 562 million of lease liabilities, which is what happens when you open premium retail, but no borrowings). Operating cash flow in the first half was CHF 255 million against CHF 89 million a year earlier, on capex of just CHF 47 million.

Inventory is the metric I check first in any apparel business, because that is where the lie shows up. Inventories rose 12.7% against reported sales growth of 14%. Inventory is growing slower than sales. Net working capital rose 11.5%. There is no channel stuffing here, and no discount cliff building in the warehouse.

5. Valuation

I value companies on a fair P/E — the multiple I believe a business of this quality, growth and durability deserves — applied to normalised earnings three years out.

The base

I do not use the company’s adjusted EPS at face value, because it adds back share-based compensation, and share-based compensation is a real cost paid in your ownership. So I build owner earnings from the guidance:

On roughly 336 million Class A-equivalent shares that is CHF 1.17, or about $1.45 at spot. Against $27.99, the stock trades at 19x owner earnings — or 17x on the company’s own adjusted basis. Enterprise value, net of the cash, is around $7.9 billion, or roughly 9x 2026 EBITDA.

The fair multiple

I set On’s fair P/E at 23.

That is what I am willing to pay for: high-teens to low-20s organic growth, a 65% gross margin that is the best in the industry, a 20% EBITDA margin, 22% return on equity, net cash, negative-ish working capital dynamics, founder control, and a replacement cycle that brings the customer back twice a year. It is below what I would pay for a software business with the same growth, because a shoe brand can lose relevance and software rarely does. It is well above a commodity consumer multiple.

The maths

Organic growth of 18% per year for three years is my working assumption — a step down from the low-20s guided for 2026, reflecting a larger base and normalising share gains. But I do not put 18% into the model, for two reasons: the franc keeps clipping several points off reported CHF results, and share-based compensation dilutes about a point a year. So I underwrite roughly 13% compounding in per-share dollar terms.

  • 2026E owner EPS: $1.45

  • 2029E owner EPS: ~$2.05

  • At a fair P/E of 23: ~$47 per share

  • From $27.99, that is a total return of about 69%, or ≈19% per year

Bull case. If the franc stops appreciating, the tariff refunds land, and operating leverage lets earnings compound at the full 18%, 2029 EPS is nearer $2.38 and fair value nearer $55 — about 25% per year. Note that this requires no multiple heroics whatsoever; 23x is not a demanding exit.

Bear case. If growth halves to 8% and the market re-rates On as a maturing brand at 15x, you get roughly $27 in three years — you lose almost nothing but you make almost nothing. That asymmetry, backed by a net-cash balance sheet, is why the position is sized as a real one rather than a speculation.

The sell-side spread tells you how contested this is. Price targets currently run from $20 at Jefferies to $73 at UBS, with a consensus around $45. When the range is that wide on a company with 65% gross margins, somebody is badly wrong. I am comfortable being on the same side as the balance sheet.

6. Risks — and why the opportunity exists at all

On 11 August the stock fell 22% in a single session. Understanding exactly why is the difference between buying a broken company and buying a mispriced one.

What actually happened. Q2 net sales of CHF 850.3 million missed consensus, and full-year constant-currency guidance came down to the low-20% range. That is it. The miss was in wholesale, which grew 12.7% at constant currency — decelerating sharply from the high-20s a year earlier.

So the market punished a company for choosing brand equity over a quarter of revenue. That is the exact trade-off I want a founder to make, and it is why the opportunity exists.

But the risks are genuine, and I hold them at the same time:

  • US consumer weakness is real. Softer sell-through in everyday running franchises is not a story management invented as cover. If it persists, the wholesale throttling stops being strategic and starts being forced. This is the single thing to watch.

  • The promotional environment could break the price discipline. On’s entire margin structure rests on not discounting. If Nike and Adidas run deep promotions through a weak season, holding the line costs volume, and abandoning it costs the moat.

  • Competition is intensifying, not easing. Nike is finally executing again. Adidas has surged back in lifestyle. Asics and Brooks are pushing hard in Asia. Hoka’s deceleration is a warning about what happens to a premium running brand that scales past its cultural moment.

  • Currency. A structurally strong franc against a company that earns in dollars is a permanent drag on reported results and, ultimately, on the dollar value of the share.

  • Fashion risk. Cloudtilt and the lifestyle push are a huge growth driver — and lifestyle sneaker demand is fickle in a way that performance running is not.

  • Leadership churn. Two CEO departures in two years is a lot, whatever the framing. If Sluis or Maguire follow, my read on the founder transition would need revisiting.

  • Valuation is not deep value. At 19x owner earnings this is a growth company at a reasonable price, not a cigar butt. It requires the growth to show up.

7. The latest quarter, and what comes next

Beyond the headline, the Q2 report contained a set of numbers that do not describe a business in trouble.

DTC grew 34.3% at constant currency to CHF 388.4 million, beating expectations in every single region, and reached a Q2 record of 45.7% of net sales. Accessories more than doubled. Cash rose CHF 185 million in the quarter alone. Gross margin hit an all-time high while paying tariffs in full.

On the innovation side: the Cloudboom Strike 2 has launched; the new SURREAL superfoam debuts in the Cloudsurfer 3 later this year; the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper with LightSpray sold out immediately, which is why Allemann now describes LightSpray as a fast-scaling commercial engine rather than a technology project.

Management’s shape for the second half is specific and worth holding them to: DTC will strongly outperform wholesale, and Q3 will be the weaker of the two quarters because that is where the deliberate wholesale reduction lands, with Q4 recovering. Guidance excludes tariff refunds entirely.

Two things to watch between now and the Q3 report on 17 November: whether US wholesale sell-through stabilises, and whether the tariff refunds begin to land. Either would move the stock. Both would move it a lot.

8. Conclusion

I bought On Holding because a very good business was priced as though it had stopped being one, for a reason that on inspection turned out to be a deliberate management choice.

The case rests on four pillars. A consumable product with a six-to-twelve-month replacement cycle, sold increasingly through channels On owns — recurring revenue without a subscription, and a structural advantage over apparel-led peers whose products simply last longer. A brand at 30% global awareness with 50 million lifetime pairs sold, meaning the runway is measured in decades rather than quarters, and with a demographic mix tilting younger, not older. Founders back in operational control of a sixteen-year-old company they still own and still build for the next decade. And a balance sheet with CHF 1.2 billion of cash and no debt, which converts every downturn from an existential question into a shopping opportunity.

Against that, you are paying 19x owner earnings for a company compounding revenue at 18–20% with the highest gross margin in its industry. At my fair P/E of 23, that is roughly 19% a year, with a bull case near 25% if the currency stops fighting and the tariff refunds arrive, and a bear case where you lose very little.

There are three ways this works. The base case is simple compounding: On keeps taking premium share, DTC mix keeps lifting margin, and the multiple stays where it is. The re-rating case is that US wholesale stabilises in the fourth quarter, the market realises the deceleration was self-inflicted and temporary, and a 17x multiple on a 20% grower is revealed as an obvious mistake. The long case — the one I actually own it for — is that apparel and accessories, currently 8% of sales and growing at 50%+, become a genuine second business, and On stops being a running shoe company at all.

I do not need the third one to work. I would just quite like it to.
